title: Certified Non-Degenerate Maximum-Likelihood Benchmarking of Quantum LDPC Decoders
authors: Michele Banfi, Marco Ferrari, Antonino Favano, Alberto Tarable, Luca Barletta
abstract: The measured logical error rate of a quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) code depends on the decoding algorithm. We develop a framework that certifies non-degenerate maximum-likelihood (ML) decoding outcomes on individual sampled shots under circuit-level noise, providing a common reference for comparing decoders and codes. Upper and lower bounds on the minimum correction cost in the true and competing logical classes establish success, failure, or an undecided outcome. Branch-and-bound search refines these intervals while retaining valid bounds under resource limits. Counting the outcomes bounds the empirical ML logical error rate, with interval width equal to the undecided fraction. Results for two bivariate bicycle codes show that best-first ordered statistics decoding (BF-OSD) tracks the non-degenerate ML benchmark closely while leaving some ML-correctable shots.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, mathematically certified framework for benchmarking quantum error-correcting codes using Maximum-Likelihood decoding. It establishes definitive success or failure by comparing rigorously derived lower and upper bounds on the minimum error costs for competing logical classes. This provides a crucial, resource-efficient tool for comparing the performance of different quantum codes.
main_problem: The paper develops a rigorous framework to certify the outcome of Maximum-Likelihood (ML) decoding for Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (QLDPC) codes.
main_result: The framework successfully establishes definitive success, failure, or undecided outcomes by comparing rigorously derived upper and lower bounds on the minimum correction cost between the true and competing logical error classes.
method: It employs advanced mathematical bounding techniques, including branch-and-bound search and Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) relaxations, to constrain the possible minimum costs without exhaustive search.
model_or_system: The study models quantum error correction using QLDPC codes operating under circuit-level noise, where decoding involves finding the minimum-cost error pattern satisfying syndrome and logical constraints.
key_observables: Minimum correction cost ($	ext{cost}(x)$), logical class ($\lambda$), and the derived bounds ($\ell_0, u_0, \ell_w, u_w$) for these costs.
important_parameters: The margin $\epsilon$ used to distinguish between success, failure, or undecided outcomes; the physical error rate $p$.
main_assumptions: The certification relies on the separation of cost intervals by a margin $\epsilon$, and the final numerical results depend on the tolerances of the underlying optimization solvers.
figures_summary: The notes mention Algorithm 1 detailing the class search procedure and Equations (12) and (13) defining the empirical error rate bounds using sampling statistics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the ML decoding objective, then introducing the bounding framework using cost intervals, refining these bounds via branch-and-bound, and finally applying the methodology to test specific codes and derive statistical guarantees on the error rate.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, mathematically rigorous tool for benchmarking quantum error correction codes, which is foundational knowledge for anyone working on fault-tolerant quantum computation or quantum information theory.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Non-degenerate ML logical error rates for [[72, 12, 6]], Nc = 6 (orange), and [[144, 12, 12]], Nc = 3 (blue). Shaded bands show joint 95% confidence intervals (13); solid lines show BF-OSD and dotted lines show BP + OSD-CS.

Fig. 2. Certification workflow for one sector. Shaded, indented steps are optional accelerations; the dotted arrow is the baseline procedure of Sec- tions III–V. Each step may lower an upper bound (u0, uw) with a verified witness or raise a lower bound (ℓ0, ℓw). The intervals are compared after every update (Proposition 1), so a sector stops as soon as it is certified. A near-tie, or a sector still open after the last step, is recorded as undecided.

Fig. 3. Separation by reduced cost, with illustrative values. (a) Columns j1, j2, j3 form the cheapest path between groups a and b of fired detectors; consecutive columns share a detector. Each weight wj splits into the charges of the fired detectors that column j flips and its reduced weight w′ j (19). (b) Every syndrome-consistent candidate pays the total charge Φ = 7. A candidate whose support connects a and b also pays at least distφ(a, b) = 0.6+1.4+1.5 = 3.5 in reduced weight (20). Since 3.5 > C −Φ = 3, it costs more than the cap C = 10 (Proposition 3).

Fig. 4. Bounding the other classes after composing two separated clusters, (22)–(23). The composed witness costs G = g1 + g2 and has class λ∗= λ1 ⊕λ2. Within the cap, a correction in another class must change the class of some cluster c, adding at least fc −gc, or contain a nonempty zero-syndrome component, adding at least wmin; any other correction costs more than C. Every other class therefore costs at least Lalt = min{C, G + Dmin}, and Lalt > G + ε decides the sector.
